title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OWN A GUN? THE QUESTION THAT COULD EXPOSE WHAT WE REALLY TRUST
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS OWN A GUN? THE QUESTION THAT COULD EXPOSE WHAT WE REALLY TRUST

When protecting your family, loving your enemies, and following Jesus collide, what does Scripture actually say? The answer may challenge both the Christian who carries a gun and the Christian who condemns everyone who does.
Imagine waking up at two in the morning.
A sound comes from downstairs.
At first, you think it's nothing. Maybe the wind. Maybe something fell.
Then you hear it again.
Footsteps.
Your wife is sleeping beside you. Your children are down the hallway. Someone is inside your home, and you have no idea what they intend to do.
Your heart begins pounding.
You have seconds to decide what happens next.
And somewhere in that terrifying moment, a question rises from the deepest part of your soul.
If I am a follower of Jesus Christ, am I allowed to use a gun to protect my family?
Now imagine another scene.

A man is angry. Someone insulted him. His pride is wounded. His hand moves toward the weapon he carries, not because anyone's life is in danger, but because something inside him refuses to be humiliated.
He calls himself a Christian, too.
Both men may own the same weapon.
Both may attend the same church.
Both may quote the same Bible.
But what is happening inside their hearts could not be more different.
And that is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the question is not simply whether a Christian can own a gun.
The deeper question is whether a Christian can possess the power to take a life while remaining completely surrendered to the One who gave His life to save His enemies.
Read that again.
This is not an article written to shame responsible gun owners. Neither is it written to baptize violence in the name of Christianity.
It is an invitation to open the Scriptures without political slogans, cultural assumptions, or selective quotations.
Because when we stand before Jesus, He will not ask whether we successfully defended our favorite political position.
He will care whether we actually followed Him.
And what Scripture reveals may surprise people on both sides.
THE SWORD JESUS TOLD HIS DISCIPLES TO BUY
There is a passage many Christians immediately mention when defending the right to own weapons.
Luke 22:36.
Jesus told His disciples:
"He that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one." (KJV)
That sounds remarkably straightforward.
Jesus Himself mentioned purchasing a sword.
But before we build an entire theology of armed self-defense around that sentence, we need to read what happened before and after it.
The Greek word translated "sword" is μάχαιρα (machaira).
It refers to a sword or large knife, often a relatively short blade, used in various practical and violent contexts in the ancient world.
Jesus was not speaking about modern firearms. Those did not exist.
Nevertheless, the passage raises a legitimate question about whether His followers could possess instruments capable of causing serious harm.
But look closely.
In Luke 22:37, Jesus connects His approaching suffering with Isaiah 53:12, explaining that He would be numbered among transgressors.
The disciples then respond:
"Lord, behold, here are two swords."
Jesus answers:
"It is enough." (Luke 22:38, KJV)
Now here is where careful interpretation matters.
Some Christians understand this exchange as evidence that Jesus permitted His disciples to possess weapons for protection during dangerous journeys.
Others understand it primarily in connection with the fulfillment of prophecy and the hostility the disciples were about to face.
Still others interpret Jesus' response as ending a conversation His disciples had misunderstood.
Faithful Christians disagree about the precise meaning.
What we cannot responsibly claim is that these verses establish an unlimited Christian right to armed violence.
Nor can we simply pretend Jesus never spoke about swords.
The passage deserves more honesty than either extreme usually gives it.
But something extraordinary happens only a few verses later.
And it changes the entire conversation.
THE NIGHT PETER DREW HIS WEAPON
The garden was dark.
Jesus had been praying.
Judas arrived with an armed crowd.
The betrayal was unfolding.
And Peter did what many frightened, protective people might instinctively do.
He reached for his sword.
John 18:10 identifies Peter as the disciple who struck the high priest's servant, cutting off his right ear.
His name was Malchus.
Think about that moment.
Peter was not defending stolen property.
He was not arguing over an insult.
He was standing before the arrest of the most innocent Man who ever lived.
If anyone could have claimed a righteous reason to resist, surely Peter would have thought he had one.
But Jesus stopped him.
"Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." (Matthew 26:52, KJV)
The Greek expression πάντες γὰρ οἱ λαβόντες μάχαιραν ἐν μαχαίρῃ ἀπολοῦνται conveys the warning that those who take up the sword will perish by the sword.
Jesus was exposing the deadly logic of violent resistance in that moment.
And then Luke records something even more astonishing.
Jesus touched the wounded servant's ear and healed him (Luke 22:51).
Peter drew blood.
Jesus restored what violence had damaged.
Peter saw an enemy.
Jesus saw a human being.
Peter tried to prevent the cross.
Jesus willingly walked toward it.
Do you see the difference?
Jesus did not merely tell Peter to put away his weapon.
He demonstrated what His kingdom looked like in the presence of an enemy.
Mercy.
Restraint.
Healing.
Obedience to the Father.
But we must also be careful not to make the passage say more than it says.
Jesus was submitting to His unique redemptive mission. He had already declared that He could appeal to His Father for heavenly protection (Matthew 26:53).
This scene clearly condemns Peter's attempt to prevent Jesus' arrest through violence.
Whether it prohibits every possible act of defensive force in every circumstance is a separate question that Christians have debated for centuries.
What cannot be debated is this:
No Christian may use Jesus as an excuse for revenge, cruelty, hatred, or reckless violence.
The hands that hold a weapon must never be ruled by a heart that refuses to obey Christ.
BUT WHAT ABOUT PROTECTING YOUR FAMILY?
This is where the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because there is a difference between wanting to hurt someone and wanting to prevent someone from hurting your child.
Imagine a mother standing between a violent attacker and her little daughter.
Imagine a father hearing his son scream for help.
Imagine an elderly believer threatened by someone determined to cause serious harm.
Are Christians required to stand aside and allow evil to proceed?
Scripture does not answer every modern self-defense scenario with a single explicit command.
But it does give us principles that matter.
Exodus 22:2–3 addresses a thief breaking into a home, distinguishing between a nighttime intrusion and a situation occurring after sunrise.
The Hebrew text uses הַבָּא בַמַּחְתֶּרֶת (habba bammachteret), referring to someone entering through a break-in.
The passage recognizes circumstances in which a confrontation may result in death without the defender bearing bloodguilt.
Yet the distinction between night and day is important. It shows that circumstances, knowledge, and the nature of the threat matter.
This was an ancient judicial law given to Israel, not a universal permission slip for modern homeowners to shoot intruders.
It cannot responsibly be interpreted as saying that every trespasser deserves death.
Human life is too sacred for that.
Proverbs 24:11 calls God's people to rescue those being taken away to death.
Psalm 82:4 says:
"Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked." (KJV)
These passages affirm a responsibility to protect vulnerable people.
But they do not prescribe firearms or authorize every possible method of intervention.
Protection is a biblical concern.
So are justice, restraint, mercy, and the preservation of life.
That is why the Christian conversation about self-defense must never begin with excitement over the possibility of using deadly force.
It must begin with grief that such force might ever become necessary.
A Christian who believes defensive force can sometimes be justified should still regard taking a human life as a terrible last resort, not a victory to celebrate.
And a Christian who believes discipleship requires nonviolent resistance must also take seriously the responsibility to protect others through whatever morally faithful means are available.
Both convictions demand courage.
Neither should be reduced to cowardice or bloodlust.
THE COMMAND MANY ARMED CHRISTIANS WOULD RATHER NOT HEAR
Now we come to the words of Jesus that should make every believer examine their heart.
Matthew 5:44.
"But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." (KJV)
Love your enemies.
Not merely tolerate them.
Not simply avoid them.
Love them.
The Greek word translated "love" is ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate), a present imperative form of agapaō.
Jesus commands His followers to love even those who oppose them.
This love does not mean approving of evil.
It does not require pretending danger is harmless.
It does mean that hatred cannot be the governing force in a Christian's response.
Now ask yourself something difficult.
If you own a firearm, have you ever imagined using it against someone who angered you?
Have you ever fantasized about making an enemy pay?
Have you ever spoken more enthusiastically about shooting an intruder than about praying for that person's salvation?
Have you ever allowed a weapon to become a symbol of your superiority, control, or personal power?
If the answer is yes, the deepest problem may not be the object in your possession.
It may be the condition of your heart.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:21–22 that God's concern reaches beyond the outward act of murder into sinful anger and contempt.
That means a person can avoid pulling a trigger and still harbor a spirit desperately in need of repentance.
And it also means that owning no weapon does not automatically make someone peaceful.
You can carry a Bible and still carry hatred.
You can reject guns and still destroy people with your words.
You can preach nonviolence while secretly enjoying the suffering of your enemies.
Jesus is not impressed by outward appearances.
He sees what we hide.
THE COMMANDMENT SAYS, "THOU SHALT NOT KILL." DOES THAT SETTLE EVERYTHING?
Many sincere believers quote Exodus 20:13 as the decisive answer.
"Thou shalt not kill." (KJV)
But the original Hebrew deserves attention.
The command reads:
לֹא תִּרְצָח (lo tirtsach)
A more precise translation in contemporary English is:
"You shall not murder."
The Hebrew verb ratsach concerns unlawful or wrongful killing, including murder, rather than every conceivable act of causing death.
This distinction matters because the Old Testament itself differentiates murder, accidental killing, judicial punishment, and warfare.
But do not miss the danger of abusing that distinction.
Explaining that the commandment prohibits murder does not automatically establish that any particular act of self-defense is morally justified.
The burden remains on the person using force to show that the action was truly necessary, proportionate, and consistent with the moral demands of Scripture.
And Christians must remember that Jesus deepened the moral seriousness of the command by confronting the anger and contempt from which violence can grow.
We cannot use Hebrew vocabulary to escape the demands of holiness.
The God who forbids murder also calls us to love our neighbor.
And even the person threatening us remains a human being made in God's image (Genesis 1:27; 9:6).
That truth should make every believer tremble before treating lethal force casually.
WHAT ABOUT ROMANS 13 AND THE GOVERNMENT'S SWORD?
Romans 13:4 says that governing authority does not bear the sword in vain.
Paul describes civil authority as having a role in restraining wrongdoing and administering justice.
Some Christians point to this passage to argue that Scripture recognizes legitimate uses of force.
That observation has merit.
But notice who Paul is discussing.
Governing authorities.
The passage is not a direct command for every private citizen to arm themselves.
And immediately before Romans 13, Paul writes:
He also commands believers to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21).
That order matters.
Paul does not give Christians permission to turn private vengeance into personal justice.
Even where defensive force may be morally permissible, revenge remains forbidden.
And this is where the modern debate often loses its spiritual center.
People become so passionate about whether they have the legal right to carry a weapon that they forget to ask whether they have developed the spiritual maturity to exercise restraint.
A LEGAL RIGHT IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A BIBLICAL COMMAND.
A government may permit something without God requiring it.
And a believer may voluntarily surrender a lawful freedom out of conscience, love, or concern for others.
Romans 14 teaches Christians to take conscience seriously in matters where believers may differ without abandoning faithfulness to God.
That does not mean every opinion is equally biblical.
It means we must distinguish explicit commands from conclusions drawn through careful moral reasoning.
A Christian should never condemn another believer as faithless merely because that believer declines to own a firearm.
Neither should a Christian automatically accuse every responsible gun owner of rejecting Jesus.
The question demands more humility than that.
WHAT IF THE GUN YOU TRUST TO PROTECT YOUR FAMILY BECOMES THE THING THAT DESTROYS IT?
There is another side to this conversation that deserves more than a passing mention.
A gun kept for protection can also create danger when it is mishandled, accessed by a child, used impulsively, stolen, or left unsecured.
Good intentions do not eliminate those risks.
Love for your family requires considering not only the threat outside your home but also the risks you introduce inside it.

If you choose to own a firearm, responsible stewardship includes obeying applicable laws, obtaining appropriate training, preventing unauthorized access, and storing it securely, generally unloaded and locked, with ammunition secured separately.
A weapon must never be accessible to a child or someone who might misuse it.
If anger, substance use, emotional instability, or threats of self-harm make access unsafe, creating distance from firearms and seeking immediate help is a responsible act of protection.
And if danger arises, escaping, creating distance, contacting emergency services, and avoiding confrontation whenever possible can save lives.
There is no shame in choosing safety over a fight.
There is no spiritual medal for escalating a confrontation you could have escaped.
Jesus said:
"Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." (Matthew 5:9, KJV)
Notice that He did not say blessed are those who win every confrontation.
He said peacemakers.
And sometimes the most courageous thing a person can do is walk away.
THE MOST DANGEROUS WEAPON MAY BE THE ONE NOBODY SEES
Let me tell you about another kind of danger.
A man goes to church every Sunday.
He sings about grace.
He quotes verses about righteousness.
He believes in defending his family.
But at home, his wife is afraid of his temper.
His children know when to remain silent.
His words can turn a peaceful evening into a battlefield.
He has never fired a gun at anyone.
But he has wounded the people he promised to protect.
And then he wonders why his family no longer feels safe around him.
Maybe that man is fictional.
Maybe he reminds you of someone you know.
Maybe, painfully, he reminds you of yourself.
If so, the answer is not to defend your image.
It is to repent.
Because the Gospel does not merely teach us when we may defend life.
It teaches us how to live a new life.
A Christian man should not be feared by his family because of his uncontrolled anger.
A Christian woman should not have to endure threats disguised as protection.
A Christian parent should never confuse intimidation with godly authority.
The fruit of the Spirit includes love, peace, patience, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
If those qualities are absent, possessing a weapon will not make someone spiritually strong.
And if a person uses a gun to threaten, dominate, or terrorize family members, that is not biblical protection.
It is abuse.

Repentance in such a situation requires stopping the harm, ensuring safety, accepting accountability, and seeking appropriate professional and pastoral help. Forgiveness must never be used to pressure victims into remaining in danger.
Jesus does not call His people to preserve appearances while others suffer.
He calls us into truth.
NOW LOOK AT THE MAN WHO CHANGED EVERYTHING
There is a reason this subject must ultimately lead us to the cross.
Jesus had the power to destroy those who came against Him.
He could have stopped His arrest.
He could have summoned heavenly help.
He could have answered cruelty with overwhelming force.
Instead, He willingly surrendered Himself to accomplish the salvation of sinners.
Isaiah 53:7 foretold the suffering Servant's submission:
"He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression כַּשֶּׂה לַטֶּבַח יוּבָל (kasseh lattebach yuval) describes one being led like a lamb to slaughter.
Jesus was not powerless.
His suffering was not evidence that evil had defeated Him.
He willingly endured the cross to redeem His people.
And while soldiers mocked Him, while His enemies humiliated Him, while nails pierced His hands, He prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." (Luke 23:34, KJV)
Consider the mercy in those words.
He prayed for forgiveness while suffering at the hands of sinners.
That is the Savior we follow.
But the cross was not merely an inspiring example of nonretaliation.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God bore our sins and accomplished redemption.
Christ died for our sins and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Through Him, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
That is why Christian ethics cannot be separated from Christian salvation.
We do not become acceptable to God by owning a gun.
We do not become acceptable to God by refusing one.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
This is where the real transformation begins.
The angry man can become gentle.
The fearful man can learn trust.
The violent man can repent.
The self-righteous man can discover humility.
The wounded person can find healing without pretending the wounds never happened.
And the person who once lived for revenge can begin learning to forgive.
Not because the past was insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the past.
SO, SHOULD CHRISTIANS OWN A GUN?
Here is the answer that may disappoint people looking for an easy slogan.
The Bible does not explicitly command Christians to own firearms.
Neither does it contain an explicit universal prohibition against every Christian possessing a firearm.
Different Christian traditions reach different conclusions about armed self-defense.
Some believe carefully limited defensive force may be morally permissible to protect innocent life.
Others, especially within historic Christian peace traditions, believe Jesus calls His disciples to reject lethal violence and pursue nonviolent protection even at great personal cost.
Both positions must be evaluated seriously against the whole counsel of Scripture.
What Scripture clearly forbids is murder, hatred, personal vengeance, and the misuse of power.
What Scripture clearly commands is love, justice, mercy, self-control, peacemaking, and trust in God.
So if you choose to own a gun, do not make it your identity.
Do not glorify violence.
Do not confuse courage with aggression.
Do not neglect the safety of your household.
Do not use Scripture to justify fantasies of retaliation.
And never imagine that your weapon makes you more faithful than a believer who chooses not to carry one.
If you choose not to own a gun, do not assume that every armed Christian is motivated by fear or hatred.
Listen carefully.
Examine the biblical arguments.
Recognize the complexity of protecting vulnerable people in a fallen world.
And whatever your conviction, remember that your ultimate security is not found in the strength of your arm, the laws of your country, or the objects you possess.
Psalm 20:7 declares:
"Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase בְּשֵׁם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ נַזְכִּיר (beshem-YHWH Eloheinu nazkir) expresses the psalmist's commitment to invoke or remember the name of the LORD our God.
In its original context, the psalm contrasts confidence in military resources with dependence upon God.
It does not forbid every practical means of protection.
But it exposes the spiritual danger of treating human power as our ultimate refuge.
And that warning is just as relevant today.
You may own a weapon.
But does your weapon own your peace?
You may be prepared for an intruder.
But are you prepared to meet your Creator?
You may know how to defend your house.
But are you allowing Jesus to rule your heart?
Because one day, every gun will be silent.
Every earthly conflict will end.
Every human life will stand before the judgment of God.
And the question of eternal importance will not be whether you won an argument about firearms.
It will be whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
The person who hurt you.
The person you still resent.
The person whose name makes your stomach tighten.
The person you secretly wish would suffer for what they did.
Maybe you have never touched a gun in your life.
But you have carried that bitterness for years.
You replay the conversation.
You imagine what you should have said.
You rehearse the humiliation.
You tell yourself you have moved on.
But the wound still speaks.
And today, perhaps Jesus is not asking you to surrender a firearm.
Perhaps He is asking you to surrender the revenge you have been holding in your heart.
Romans 12:19 reminds us that vengeance belongs to God.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending injustice never happened.
It does not mean removing wise boundaries.
It does not mean returning to an abusive situation.
It means refusing to make hatred the master of your soul.
And sometimes that surrender begins with a prayer so small that nobody else hears it.

"Lord Jesus, I am angry. I am afraid. I have trusted my own strength more than I have trusted You. Teach me to protect without hatred, to act without revenge, and to love without surrendering truth. Forgive my sins. Change my heart. Make me more like You."
Maybe that prayer is for you.
Maybe it is for someone you love.
Maybe it is for a person who has been carrying pain beneath a smile for longer than anyone realizes.
If this article exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
Bring it before Jesus.
He already knows.
And His grace is sufficient to meet repentant sinners in the places they are most ashamed to reveal.
I also want to hear from you.
Should Christians own a gun? Can armed self-defense and the command to love our enemies be reconciled, or do you believe following Jesus requires a commitment to nonviolence?
Your testimony may encourage someone who thought they were the only person wrestling with these questions.
Because this ministry is not meant to win arguments while losing souls.
We want to see lives transformed by the Gospel.
And that is also why I want to personally invite you to go deeper.
These resources are meant to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand sound doctrine, and grow in their daily walk with the Lord.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry takes real work and real resources.
Please continue honoring your responsibilities to your family and local church.
But if you have the means and the desire to help this ministry reach more people, your faithful support can make a meaningful difference.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who help make the work possible.
God sees faithfulness that never appears on a payment receipt.
Come closer to Jesus.
Open your Bible.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Protect life.
Reject hatred.
Walk in truth.
And let the Holy Spirit continue the transforming work that only God can accomplish.
Because at the end of everything, Christianity is not about proving that we are strong enough to defeat our enemies.
It is about belonging to the Savior who loved us when we were His enemies.
The One who could have called down judgment chose to bear the cross.
The One who was mocked became the hope of sinners.
The One who was crucified rose from the dead.
And the One who conquered the grave is still changing hearts today.
So whether there is a gun in your home or not, make sure there is no throne in your heart reserved for fear, pride, revenge, or violence.
That throne belongs to Jesus.
You can spend your whole life preparing to stop an enemy at your door, only to discover that the hatred destroying your peace was already living inside your heart.
